Thomas: bro sorry, this week for sure

Noor: So what, I just trust everyone?

Noor: And Sana? She always pays back.
Api: Then Sana's fine. That's the point.

qa.q: How much money did Noor lend Thomas?
qa.a: Noor lent Thomas 2,000 for the trip.

qa.q: How did Noor feel after two weeks with no reply from Thomas?
qa.a: Noor felt betrayed and stupid, and wanted to stop lending anyone anything again.

qa.q: What does Api suggest Noor do next, and why is it wiser than trusting nobody?
qa.a: Api says to trust people who've shown it and start small, so Noor can still help someone like Sana who always pays back, while saying no to Thomas.

qa.q: How might Sana be affected if Noor stopped trusting everyone?
qa.a: Sana, who always pays back, would be treated as if she had done something wrong, which would feel unfair to her.

grounding: A student whose loan is not repaid feels betrayed and foolish, and learns from an older sister to trust more carefully rather than not at all.

passage: Bhupen spent six weeks on his botany project at the college in Tezpur, walking the tea-garden edges every morning to count ferns. Alka, from the next village bus stop, asked to see his draft. 'Just to get the format right,' she said. He sent it the same night. At the seminar, Alka presented first. Her slides had his fern counts, his map, even his joke about the goat eating a sample. Bhupen sat very still while the teacher praised her. On the bus home he watched the paddy fields and felt like a fool. For a week he didn't reply to anyone's messages. Then his friend Moni asked for help with graphs. He almost said no. Instead he helped her in the library, where the teacher could see, and kept his own files dated. He hadn't stopped helping. He'd just started helping more carefully.

qa.q: What did Alka ask Bhupen for?
qa.a: Alka asked to see his draft, 'just to get the format right'.

qa.q: How did Bhupen feel on the bus home after the seminar?
qa.a: He felt betrayed and like a fool for trusting Alka, sitting silent and watching the paddy fields.

qa.q: What choice did Bhupen make when Moni asked for help, and why was it a good one?
qa.a: He helped her, but in the library where the teacher could see and with his own files dated, so he stayed generous while protecting his work.

qa.q: How might Moni be affected if Bhupen had decided never to share again?
qa.a: Moni, who had done nothing wrong, would have lost help with her graphs because of what Alka did.

grounding: A student whose project draft is copied feels betrayed and gullible, then learns to share more carefully instead of refusing to trust anyone.

passage: In their shared flat in Lisbon, Chidi lent Paulo two hundred euros in September. Paulo said his scholarship payment was late and he'd return it in a fortnight. November came. Paulo bought concert tickets, posted photos from a weekend trip, and changed the subject whenever Chidi mentioned money. One evening Chidi sat on his narrow bed, looking at his bank app, feeling foolish. His mother had always said he trusted too easily. Maybe she was right. Maybe he should trust no one. The next week a classmate, Lucía, asked to borrow his lecture notes before an exam. Chidi hesitated, then said yes, and added, 'Can I have them back Thursday?' She returned them Wednesday, with a thank-you chocolate. Chidi smiled. He still wanted the money back from Paulo. But one person had not decided who everyone else was.

qa.q: How much did Chidi lend Paulo?
qa.a: Chidi lent Paulo two hundred euros in September.

qa.q: What was Chidi feeling when he sat on his bed looking at his bank app?
qa.a: He felt foolish and betrayed, and wondered whether his mother was right that he trusted too easily.

qa.q: What did Chidi do differently when Lucía asked for his notes, and why did it work?
qa.a: He lent them but asked for them back by Thursday, trusting her with a clear limit, and she returned them early.

qa.q: How might Lucía have been treated if Chidi had decided to trust no one?
qa.a: Lucía might have been refused the notes before her exam, even though she had done nothing to deserve suspicion.

grounding: A student let down over an unpaid loan feels gullible, and then chooses to trust more carefully, with clear limits, rather than trust no one.

passage: In the placement cell's waiting room, Sachin heard his own sentence read aloud. "I first fell in love with bridges when..." It was from his cover letter. Except the recruiter was holding Manjula's file. Two weeks earlier, in the hostel study room, Manjula had asked to "just look at the format". He'd emailed it without a second thought. Now his face burned. He felt stupid more than angry. That night he sat on his bed, laptop open, deleting shared folders one by one. His roommate looked up. "Going to trust nobody now?" Sachin stopped. "No. Just... share the format, not the letter. And watch what people do with small things first." He left one folder open: the group study notes.

qa.q: What had Manjula asked to look at?
qa.a: Just the format of Sachin's cover letter.

qa.q: What was Sachin feeling when his sentence was read from Manjula's file?
qa.a: His face burned; he felt stupid and gullible more than angry, betrayed by how easily he had shared.

qa.q: What did Sachin decide when his roommate asked the question, and why is it wiser than trusting nobody?
qa.a: To share formats rather than finished letters and watch how people handle small things first, which protects him without cutting off shared help like the group notes.

qa.q: How might the roommate see Sachin deleting folders one by one?
qa.a: The roommate worries Sachin might shut everyone out after one betrayal, which is why the question about trusting nobody is asked.

grounding: A student whose shared cover letter is copied feels betrayed and gullible, then decides to trust more carefully rather than not at all.

passage:
Chetan,
I'm writing because saying it out loud would come out as shouting.
In September you borrowed my camera for your cousin's wedding. "Back by Monday," you said. It's December. When I asked last week, you said it was "at home somewhere", and then I saw it in your photos from the beach trip.
I bought that camera with my first stipend. I lent it because you're my friend, and because when I was new at college you walked me to the bus stand every evening for a month. I trusted that person.
Honestly, I feel stupid. Like everyone else saw this coming except me.
I'm not going to stop lending things to people. But I'll lend smaller things first, and ask for dates in writing. Please return the camera by Sunday.
Pallavi

qa.q: When did Chetan say the camera would be back?
qa.a: By Monday.

qa.q: What does "Honestly, I feel stupid" reveal about Pallavi?
qa.a: Pallavi feels betrayed and gullible, as if everyone else could have predicted this except Pallavi.

qa.q: What choice does Pallavi make about trusting people in future?
qa.a: To keep lending, but smaller things first and with dates in writing, trusting more carefully rather than trusting nobody.

qa.q: How might Chetan feel reading the line about the bus stand?
qa.a: Chetan may feel ashamed, reminded that Pallavi's trust grew from Chetan's own earlier kindness, which makes the let-down sharper.

grounding: A student who lent a camera to a friend feels betrayed and gullible when it isn't returned, and decides to trust more carefully rather than not at all.

passage:
In the small college at Karad, Lokesh's handwritten physics notes were famous: neat diagrams, every derivation. When Nikita, from the next bench, said she'd missed a month for her grandmother's illness, he handed over the whole notebook without thinking.
Two weeks later he walked into the xerox shop near the bus stand and saw stacks of his own pages on sale, twenty rupees a set. Nikita had lent the notebook to the shopkeeper. It came back with tea rings on the cover.
Lokesh sat on the college wall that evening, burning with embarrassment. How had he not seen it? He thought about never lending anything again. Then he thought of Vinod, who had borrowed his notes all last year and returned them every Monday.

qa.q: How much was each set of notes sold for at the xerox shop?
qa.a: Twenty rupees a set.

qa.q: What was Lokesh feeling on the college wall that evening?
qa.a: He felt betrayed and embarrassed, even gullible, for handing over his notebook so easily.

qa.q: What could Lokesh do next time someone asks for his notes?
qa.a: Lend to people with a track record like Vinod, or share a chapter first, instead of refusing everyone.

qa.q: What would change if Nikita had asked before giving the notebook to the shop?
qa.a: Lokesh could have agreed or refused, and his trust in Nikita might have stayed intact.

grounding: Shows a student whose lent notes were misused feeling betrayed and gullible, then weighing careful trust against trusting nobody.

passage:
Jana had saved for her camera through two summers of waitressing in Leipzig. When Lars, from her film course, begged to borrow it for a weekend shoot, she hesitated, then said yes; he had been so friendly all term.
It came back on Tuesday with a cracked lens and a shrug. "It was like that when I got it," Lars said, not looking at her. Jana knew it wasn't.
That night she sat on her bed with the camera in her lap, feeling foolish more than angry. Her flatmate Ines asked if she would ever lend it again. "To you, yes," Jana said. "To someone who's been nice for one term? I'll wait longer next time."

qa.q: What was wrong with the camera when it came back?
qa.a: It came back with a cracked lens.

qa.q: Why did Jana feel foolish more than angry?
qa.a: She felt ashamed of trusting too quickly, since Lars's friendliness for one term had seemed like enough.

qa.q: What is wise about Jana's answer to Ines?
qa.a: She keeps trusting people with a proven record while waiting longer with newer friends, instead of trusting nobody.

qa.q: What would change if Lars had admitted the damage?
qa.a: Jana might still be upset, but honesty could have saved some trust and opened a way to repair it.

grounding: Shows a student let down by someone who damaged a borrowed camera, feeling gullible, and choosing to trust more slowly rather than not at all.

passage:
In the university library, Nirmala spent two months writing her term paper on water policy. When Francis asked to "just look at it for ideas," she emailed him the draft.
A week later, the professor returned the papers. Francis had used her structure, her examples and even one of her sentences. His paper got a better grade.
Nirmala sat in the reading room, feeling stupid and betrayed. Why did I trust him? she thought. She felt like never sharing anything again.
That evening she told her friend in the next hostel room. Her friend said, "Don't stop sharing. Just share with people who've shown they're fair. And report the copying."
The next day Nirmala went to the professor.

qa.q: How long did Nirmala spend on her term paper?
qa.a: She spent two months writing it.

qa.q: What was Nirmala feeling in the reading room?
qa.a: She felt stupid and betrayed, wondering why she had trusted Francis.

qa.q: What advice did her friend give, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Keep sharing only with people who have shown fairness and report the copying, so Nirmala trusts more carefully instead of trusting nobody.

qa.q: How might Francis feel when the professor learns about the copying?
qa.a: Francis may feel caught and anxious, facing the consequences of misusing Nirmala's draft.

grounding: Shows a student who shared a draft with someone who misused it feeling betrayed and gullible, and learning to trust more carefully rather than not at all.

passage:
Dear Santosh,
It's been four months since you borrowed money for your exam fees. You said you'd return it in two weeks. I've messaged three times. You've read the messages and not replied.
I'm Tanvir, and I'm writing this not to shout, but because I need to say it. I feel foolish. I trusted you because we were roommates, and I thought that meant something.
I'm not going to stop helping people. But next time, I'll lend only what I can afford to lose, and only to people who've shown they can keep their word.
If you can return even part of it, please do. And if something's wrong, just tell me.

qa.q: How long ago did Santosh borrow the money?
qa.a: It's been four months.

qa.q: What is Tanvir feeling while writing this letter?
qa.a: Tanvir feels foolish and betrayed, having trusted Santosh because they were roommates.

qa.q: What has Tanvir learned about trust?
qa.a: Tanvir has learned to trust more carefully, lending only what can be lost and only to people who've shown they keep their word.

qa.q: How might Santosh feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Santosh may feel ashamed and guilty, or worried if something is really wrong.

grounding: Shows a student who lent money to a roommate who never returned it, feeling betrayed and gullible, and learning to trust more carefully.

passage:
You want to know why I'm careful now? I'm Joseph. In second year, I shared my scholarship essay with Zainab. She said she was stuck and wanted to see how I'd started.
Two weeks later, the results came. Her essay had my opening story, my structure, almost my exact conclusion. She got the scholarship. I didn't.
I felt so stupid. I'd trusted her because she sat next to me in lectures. I told myself: never again, trust no one.
But that didn't last. A month later, my friend Ashok asked for help with his project. He'd always paid back favours. I helped him.
I still share. I just check who I'm sharing with.

qa.q: What did Joseph share with Zainab?
qa.a: Joseph shared the scholarship essay.

qa.q: What did Joseph feel when the results came?
qa.a: Joseph felt stupid and betrayed, having trusted Zainab only because she sat next to Joseph.

qa.q: What did Joseph learn about trust?
qa.a: To trust more carefully by checking a person's record, like Ashok's, rather than trusting nobody.

qa.q: How might Zainab see her own actions?
qa.a: She may tell herself she only borrowed ideas, not realising or admitting how much she hurt Joseph.

grounding: Shows a student whose shared essay was misused, feeling betrayed, and learning to trust carefully rather than trust no one.

passage: Varun, you've gone quiet since your friend didn't pay you back. Let me tell you something from my hostel days. When I was a girl of twenty, my hostel-mate Kamini said her mother was sick and she needed money for the train. I gave her most of what I had for the month. She promised to return it in a week. A week passed. A month. She avoided me in the mess. I felt like such a fool, Varun. I cried to my mother on the phone. For a while, I said I'd never lend anything to anyone. But then I saw that wasn't me either. So I became careful. I got to know people first. I trusted more slowly. That's what Himani Maasi learned.

qa.q: What did Kamini say she needed money for?
qa.a: The train, because her mother was sick.

qa.q: How did young Himani feel when Kamini avoided her?
qa.a: She felt betrayed and foolish, even crying to her mother on the phone.

qa.q: What choice in the story shows the lesson Himani learned?
qa.a: Instead of refusing to trust anyone, she chose to get to know people first and trust more slowly.

qa.q: How might Kamini have felt avoiding Himani in the mess?
qa.a: Kamini may have felt ashamed and guilty, unable to face Himani.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling being let down after lending money as a student, and learning to trust more carefully.

passage: It rained through the whole of exam week, and Jeevan's only laptop was his lifeline. Binita, from his class, asked to borrow it for one evening to finish her assignment; hers had broken. He hesitated, then said yes. She kept it three days, didn't answer messages, and returned it with a cracked screen and someone else's games installed. "My brother used it, sorry," she said, not meeting his eyes. Jeevan had to write his last assignment in the computer lab, queuing in the wet corridor. He felt betrayed and gullible. That weekend a junior asked to borrow it too. Jeevan paused. "You can use it here, with me, for an hour." He still wanted to help. He just wasn't handing things over blindly anymore.

qa.q: What was wrong with the laptop when Binita returned it?
qa.a: It had a cracked screen and someone else's games installed.

qa.q: How did Jeevan feel after getting the laptop back?
qa.a: He felt betrayed and gullible, having trusted Binita during his most important week.

qa.q: What did Jeevan offer the junior instead of lending the laptop?
qa.a: To use it with him for an hour, which let him help while trusting more carefully.

qa.q: How might Binita feel returning the laptop?
qa.a: Binita likely felt guilty and embarrassed, which is why she didn't meet his eyes.

grounding: Illustrates a student whose trust was misused feeling betrayed, then choosing to trust more carefully rather than not at all.

passage: The week before Christmas, while his hostel room in Pune was strung with paper stars, Francis sent Naveen his marketing project draft. 'Just to see the format,' Naveen had said. 'I'm totally lost.' In January the professor called them both in. Whole paragraphs of Naveen's report matched Francis's, down to a typo in the third table. Naveen stared at the floor and said nothing. Francis walked back to the hostel feeling stupid more than angry. He had believed every word. That night his roommate Aby asked to see his notes for the statistics exam. Francis's first thought was no, not to anyone, ever again. Instead he pulled his chair over, opened the notebook, and they worked through the problems together at the desk. He just didn't send the file.

qa.q: What matched between Naveen's report and Francis's?
qa.a: Whole paragraphs matched, down to a typo in the third table.

qa.q: How did Francis feel walking back to the hostel, and why?
qa.a: He felt betrayed and gullible, more stupid than angry, because he had believed Naveen's 'just to see the format' completely.

qa.q: How did Francis change the way he trusts, and why was that wise?
qa.a: He still helped Aby, but by working through the notes together instead of sending the file; that is careful trust rather than trusting nobody.

qa.q: What would it have been like for Aby if Francis had refused outright?
qa.a: Aby, who had done nothing wrong, would have been shut out and confused, paying for someone else's betrayal.

grounding: Shows a student whose shared draft is copied, who feels betrayed and gullible, and who then trusts more carefully instead of refusing everyone.
